definition.text: Biological pest control is the use of living organisms to control pests, whether animals, weeds or disease-causing organisms.

facts.text: It works through predation, parasitism and plant-eating, usually with people actively managing it, and can be part of integrated pest management.
The first known record comes from China around 304 AD, where citrus growers bought nests of predatory ants to protect their fruit.
Modern biological control began in the US in the 1870s, when state entomologists started handing out parasitoids to fight crop pests.
Agents include predators such as lady beetles, parasitoid wasps and flies, and disease organisms such as bacteria, fungi and viruses.
Bacillus thuringiensis, a soil bacterium, is the most widely used bacterial control agent, and its genes have been put into transgenic crops.
Biological control can reduce the economic losses caused by pests, disease carriers and invasive species.
Using natural enemies instead of pesticides can also cut agricultural pollution.

definition.text: Biological control comes in three basic strategies: importation, augmentation and conservation of natural enemies.

facts.text: Importation, or classical control, brings a pest's natural enemies into a new place where they did not live before.
Augmentation releases extra natural enemies: a few at intervals to prevent outbreaks (inoculative), or many at once to knock a pest down fast (inundative).
Early importations were often unofficial, and some introduced species became serious pests themselves.

definition.text: Conservation biological control protects and encourages the natural enemies of pests that already live in an area.

facts.text: Nectar plants grown on rice field borders cut planthopper pests 10- to 100-fold, so farmers sprayed 70% less insecticide and gained 5% in yield.
Changing cropping systems to favour natural enemies is called habitat manipulation, for example with hedgerows, shelterbelts or beetle banks.
A meter-wide strip of tussock grass in the middle of English fields let aphid predators overwinter there and improved control.

definition.text: An introduced control agent can harm biodiversity by attacking native species as well as the pest it was meant for.

facts.text: Vertebrates tend to eat many kinds of food and seldom make good control agents; many classic failures involve them.
Cane toads released in Australia in 1935 could not reach the cane beetles, spread fast instead and harmed native frogs and predators.

definition.text: Erosion control is the practice of preventing or limiting soil loss to wind or water on farms, building sites, coasts and riverbanks.

facts.text: Good erosion control manages surface runoff and helps prevent water pollution, soil loss, habitat loss and damage to property.
Controls often put up a physical barrier, such as plants or rock, to absorb some of the energy of the wind or water.
Bank erosion is natural, and without it rivers would not meander, but people often fix riverbanks with riprap or gabions.
Since the 1920s and 1930s scientists have built mathematical models of soil erosion, growing into large computer models by the 1970s.
In landslide-prone areas forests can hold soils in place and prevent damage, injury and loss of life.
Mangroves' coastal protection and erosion control can save spending on costly civil engineering projects.

definition.text: Pollination is the moving of pollen from the male part of a flower to the female part, which lets the plant make seeds.

facts.text: Pollen can be carried by animals such as bees, beetles, butterflies, birds and bats, or by wind and water.
Between 100,000 and 200,000 animal species pollinate the world's 250,000 species of flowering plant, most of them insects.
About 80% of flowering plants rely on living pollinators.
Farms closer to natural habitat get more pollinator visits and higher crop yields.
Three quarters of the plant species that feed the world need pollinators, and insect-pollinated crops are worth over 200 billion dollars.
Animal pollination keeps plants genetically varied because it allows cross-breeding rather than self-breeding.

definition.text: Beekeepers rent their honeybee colonies to farmers for a fee, turning crop pollination into a service sold in a market.

facts.text: Honeybees do most pollination of the crops people eat, giving between $235 and $577 billion of benefits to global food production.
As of 2016, pollination rentals made up 41% of an average US beekeeper's revenue, the largest share of their income.
Pollination by beekeepers' bees is a positive externality that the market has managed to pay for.
The almond industry uses up to 82% of the pollination market, and each February around 60% of US bee colonies are moved to California's Central Valley.
Mixing hives spreads disease to wild bees too, a negative externality that reduces biodiversity.
In 2016 an almond colony earned $165 in rent, about three times other crops, yet once upkeep is counted almond pollination is barely profitable.

definition.text: Biotic pollination uses living animals to carry pollen, while abiotic pollination relies on wind, water or rain.

facts.text: Some 98% of abiotic pollination is by wind.
Abiotic pollination lets a plant spend its energy on pollen rather than on flowers and nectar to attract animals.
Some plants use both kinds, such as an orchid pollinated by rain or butterflies depending on conditions.

definition.text: Many farm crops depend on pollinators, while the main staple grains such as wheat, maize and rice are pollinated by wind or by themselves.

facts.text: Among the top 15 crops in 2013, slightly over 10% of the human plant diet (211 of 1916 kcal per person per day) depended on insect pollination.
Managed US beehives fell from close to 6 million after WWII to under 2.5 million, while bee-pollinated crop area grew over 300%.
About one million hives, nearly half of US honey bees, are trucked to California almond orchards each spring.

definition.text: A plant–pollinator network is the web of links formed when many pollinator species visit many plant species.

facts.text: These networks have a strikingly similar structure on different continents, even with entirely different species.
Network structure may shape how pollinator communities respond to harsher conditions.
